hook_text: You were taught Napoleon was tiny. He was average height for his time.
Medieval people didn’t think the Earth was flat. Educated Europeans knew it was round.
Vikings never wore horned helmets. Blame an 1876 opera.
Columbus didn’t prove the Earth was round. Nobody serious doubted it.
Medieval people drank water too. The “only beer” story is a myth.
Marie Antoinette probably never said ‘Let them eat cake.’
The Great Wall isn’t visible from the Moon with the naked eye.
Gladiator fights didn’t always end in death. Many fighters walked away.
Paul Revere never shouted ‘The British are coming!’
Thomas Edison didn’t invent the light bulb. He improved it.
Ancient Greek statues weren’t plain white. Many were brightly painted.
You think Cleopatra was Egyptian. Her family was Macedonian Greek.
Franklin never proposed the turkey as national bird. He praised it in a letter.
Knights didn’t need cranes to climb onto their horses.
Magellan didn’t sail around the world. He died before the voyage ended.
On December 17, 1903, a powered plane flew for twelve seconds.
On May 24, 1844, a message crossed forty miles in an instant.
On September 2, 1666, a London bakery fire began. It burned four days.
On September 2, 1752, Britons went to bed and woke up on the 14th.
On October 4, 1957, a metal ball started beeping from orbit.
On November 9, 1989, a border opened that had split a city for decades.
On May 10, 1869, a golden spike finished the first transcontinental railroad.
In July 1799, soldiers in Egypt found the stone that unlocked hieroglyphs.
On August 3, 1492, three ships left Spain. Nobody aboard expected America.
On June 15, 1215, a king agreed to rules he didn’t plan to keep.
On November 8, 1895, a German lab screen glowed when it shouldn’t have.
On January 10, 1863, London’s first underground trains carried passengers.
On May 6, 1840, the world’s first postage stamp became valid.
On October 4, 1582, parts of Europe went to bed. Tomorrow was October 15.
On December 14, 1911, a team reached the South Pole first.
If you were a knocker-upper in 1900, your job was waking people up.
If you were a medieval scribe, one book could take you months.
If you were a Roman soldier, you also had to be a builder.
If you were a sailor in the 1700s, lemons could save your life.
If you were a lamplighter in 1850, you lit a whole street by hand.
If you built pyramids in Egypt, your wages included bread and beer.
If you were a telegraph operator in 1870, you could hear words in clicks.
If you were a medieval peasant, church feast days gave you days off.
If you were a Victorian kitchen dog, your job was turning the roast.
If you were a ship’s navigator in 1600, longitude was mostly estimation.
If you were a Roman shopper, lunch came from a street counter.
If you were a Tudor-era Londoner, the law said what fabric you could wear.
If you were an ice cutter in 1850, winter was your harvest season.
If you were a lighthouse keeper in 1880, you trimmed wicks all night.
If you were a London postman in 1900, you delivered several times a day.
This iron helmet from Norway has no horns. That’s the point.
This broken stone slab let people read hieroglyphs again.
This corroded bronze lump from a shipwreck turned out to be a gear machine.
This blurry rooftop view is the oldest surviving camera photograph.
This book has been studied for a century. Nobody can read it.
These chess pieces were carved from walrus ivory and found on a Scottish island.
This clock solved a problem that sank ships for centuries.
This tiny black stamp changed how the whole world sends letters.
This golden spike was driven in, then pulled straight back out.
This X-ray of a hand shocked the world in 1896.
This one carved word is nearly all the Roanoke colonists left behind.
This old map shows California as an island. Mapmakers copied it for decades.
This Roman dome has stood for nearly 1,900 years without steel inside.
This Bible was printed with movable metal type around 1455.
This tin can came with no can opener. That arrived decades later.

hook_text: Magna Carta was cancelled within ten weeks. It survived anyway.

hook_type: How close it came / near miss
hook_text: Gutenberg printed his famous Bible, then lost his workshop in a lawsuit.

hook_type: How close it came / near miss
hook_text: The clockmaker who solved longitude nearly never got paid for it.

hook_type: How close it came / near miss
hook_text: The Rosetta Stone was found by French soldiers. Britain ended up with it.

hook_type: How close it came / near miss
hook_text: The Library of Congress burned in 1814. A former president’s books replaced it.

hook_type: How close it came / near miss
hook_text: In 1911, the Mona Lisa vanished from the Louvre for over two years.

hook_type: How close it came / near miss
hook_text: In 1666, London helped stop a giant fire by blowing up its own houses.

hook_type: How close it came / near miss
hook_text: The Wright Flyer first flew in America but spent twenty years in London.

hook_type: How close it came / near miss
hook_text: The ancient gear machine sat in a museum for months before anyone noticed.

hook_type: How close it came / near miss
hook_text: The supply ship for Roanoke arrived three years late. Everyone was gone.

hook_type: How close it came / near miss
hook_text: Five ships left Spain in 1519. Only one sailed all the way around.

hook_type: How close it came / near miss
hook_text: In the 1790s, the Bayeux Tapestry was reportedly almost used as a wagon cover.

hook_type: How close it came / near miss
hook_text: The first big telegraph line was meant to run underground. The buried wire failed.

hook_type: How close it came / near miss
hook_text: The Lewis and Clark expedition lost only one man, most likely to appendicitis.
In 1830, the person receiving a letter in Britain usually paid for it.
In 1840, many British towns kept their own local time.
In 1820, summer ice was a luxury cut from frozen New England ponds.
In 1865, British law limited steam road vehicles to four miles an hour.
In 1400, almost every book in Europe was copied by hand.
In 1700, sailors couldn’t reliably tell how far east or west they were.
In 1894, nobody had ever seen inside a living body without surgery.
In 1700, a Londoner might pay a tax on how many windows they had.
In 1850, London’s sewage flowed straight into the river people drank from.
In 79 AD, many Pompeii residents grabbed hot food from street counters.
In 1750, England’s legal year still began on March 25.
In 1900, nobody had ever stood at the South Pole.
In 1890, nobody had ever flown in a powered, controlled airplane.
In 1314, playing football in London’s streets could get you jailed.
In 1950, nothing made by humans had ever orbited Earth.
Before the Mayflower, an English colony vanished from the map.
In 1858, the Thames smelled so bad Parliament worked behind chemical-soaked curtains.
In the 1400s, Chinese fleets reached East Africa, decades before Columbus sailed.
In 1883, a volcano’s blast was heard almost 3,000 miles away.
In 1816, Europe and North America had a ‘year without a summer.’
In 1814, a flood of beer swept through a London street.
Pigs and other animals were once put on trial in European courts.
In 1859, telegraph wires sparked during a giant solar storm.
In the 1560s, Spanish galleons began crossing the Pacific with silver each year.
Roman engineers built tens of thousands of miles of paved roads.
Turnspit dogs once ran in wheels to roast meat in British kitchens.
In 1783, a sheep, a duck and a rooster flew in a hot-air balloon.
A Viking settlement in Canada sat forgotten until the 1960s.
Medieval London had a bridge lined with houses and shops.
Around 1259 BC, Egypt and the Hittites signed a written peace treaty.
Cleopatra lived closer to the Moon landing than to the Great Pyramid’s construction.
Cologne Cathedral took over 600 years to finish.
About 18 of roughly 270 men finished the first voyage around the world.
The first photograph needed an exposure of many hours, maybe days.
Britain’s window tax lasted 155 years.
The first powered flight covered 120 feet, less than a jumbo jet’s wingspan.
The Pantheon’s dome is about 43 meters across, and it’s unreinforced concrete.
Sputnik circled Earth about once every 96 minutes.
Gutenberg printed about 180 Bibles. Fewer than 50 survive today.
Measured with all its branches, the Great Wall runs over 13,000 miles.
Roanoke’s colonists numbered about 115. None were ever found.
The Voynich manuscript has about 240 pages nobody can read.
Zheng He’s first fleet reportedly carried around 27,000 people.
Ancient Rome’s Colosseum could seat about 50,000 people.
On an 81-day voyage to Jamaica, Harrison’s watch lost about five seconds.
Russian men once paid a tax to keep their beards.
England’s Tudor laws decided who could wear purple silk.
In 1386, a French town reportedly dressed a pig in clothes for its trial.
Roman laundries collected urine on purpose, and the emperor taxed it.
England’s kings banned football so men would practice archery instead.
British drivers once needed someone walking ahead waving a red flag.
In 1795, Britain made anyone using hair powder buy a yearly certificate.
In 1266, English law tied the weight of a loaf to grain prices.
During Saturnalia, Roman masters sometimes served dinner to the people they enslaved.
Some medieval church courts heard cases against insects that ate crops.
In Victorian Britain, widows were expected to wear mourning clothes for about two years.
Tudor England fined people for not going to church.
Ancient Athens could vote to banish a citizen for ten years, no crime needed.
In Edo-period Japan, only samurai could legally wear two swords.
A 1336 English law limited most people’s meals to two courses.
An entire English colony disappeared, leaving one word carved on a post.
Thousands of Indus Valley seals survive. Nobody can read a single one.
A ship was found sailing with nobody aboard. The crew was never found.
Amelia Earhart’s plane vanished in 1937, and searchers never found it.
A Roman legion vanishes from the records. Nobody knows exactly what happened.
The Library of Alexandria’s lost books: nobody knows how many there were.
One medieval book is written in a script no one has cracked.
Where is Cleopatra buried? Archaeologists still don’t know.
Leonardo’s lost Florence mural may lie behind a later wall. Nobody has proven it.
Genghis Khan’s tomb has never been found.
Shakespeare co-wrote a play called Cardenio. No copy of it survives.
What caused the 1518 dancing plague? Historians still argue about it.
Who built the ancient gear machine found off Antikythera? Nobody knows.
Why did the Maya leave their great southern cities? There’s still no single answer.
The Phaistos Disc’s spiral of symbols has never been deciphered.
